correctness.rationale: For three candidates and two seats, first choice maximizes support and doubled second-stage marginal equals \(2v(b)-v(a,b)\). Seven nonempty ballot types and unordered multisets exhaust every anonymous residual electorate and unordered two-voter coalition: \(28\binom{n+4}{6}\) cases for each total size n. Exact comparison finds zero violations for \(3\le n\le11\) and exactly six for \(n=12\); all six are one S3 orbit. The representative has abstention outputs {AB,AC} but participating output {AB}, meeting both universal weak and existential strict Kelly comparisons. Adjoining universal-approval voters adds common first-stage 1 and second-stage doubled marginal 1; hence the same failure persists for \(n\ge12\). The packaged rational PAV evaluator separately confirms the representative and six instances. Exhaustive finite tests address a finite cutoff, not untested infinite models.

originality.rationale: The most relevant 2023 paper proves group participation for globally optimizing ABC scoring rules and individual participation for sequential Thiele with two seats; neither implies group participation for two-seat greedy PAV, and the inspected text did not state this sharp two-person threshold or its six-instance orbit. The survey defines the greedy PAV procedure but does not assert the coalition theorem. Sequential-rule axiomatization does not give the numerical cutoff. Published research records found nearby no-show minima for ranked single-winner rules (Coombs, Bucklin, IRV), whose assumptions and conclusions do not imply the present approval two-seat case. This is a best-knowledge scientific comparison, not a guarantee of priority.

value.rationale: The small \(k=2\) case is mathematically motivated by the established exception for individual participation of greedy Thiele rules, so asking whether it extends to coalitions is natural. Two abstainers are the smallest group beyond that theorem and three candidates the smallest nontrivial two-seat election. The exact first electorate size 12 and the unique six-case symmetry orbit give a complete finite boundary and transparent mechanism: coalition absence makes a preferred committee available via a tie while never making any member worse off. This advances the structural separation rather than merely counting an arbitrary sample; the tie and preference-extension sensitivity are made explicit.
